Growth in Cubera snapper Lutjanus cyanopterus, a large-bodied member of the Lutjanidae, proceeds toward an ultimate fork length of 160 cm [Li = 160 cm], a size that places it among the largest snapper species in the western Atlantic. The corresponding ultimate wet weight, derived from length–weight regressions on mature individuals, has been estimated at 47,664 grams [Wwi = 47,664 grams], reflecting the substantial somatic investment required to attain such dimensions. Juvenile specimens recruit to mangrove and seagrass habitats, where they undergo a period of accelerated mass gain before transitioning to deeper reef environments as sub-adults. Tagging studies indicate that growth rates are strongly influenced by local prey abundance and water temperature, with individuals in productive nursery grounds reaching fork lengths exceeding 100 centimeters within their first decade. The species exhibits a moderately slow life history, with considerable energy devoted to structural growth before the onset of gonadal maturation.

Sexual maturity in Lutjanus cyanopterus is attained at a fork length of 80 cm [Lp = 80 cm], a threshold that marks the transition from the sub-adult to the reproductively viable phase. The body mass associated with this length is considerable; individuals at the onset of puberty weigh approximately 6,041 grams [Wwp = approximately 6,041 grams], based on the same length–weight scaling relationship used for asymptotic adults. This size at maturity is consistent with the pattern observed in other iteroparous tropical reef fishes, where delayed maturation allows the accumulation of sufficient energy reserves for repeated spawning events. Histological examination of gonadal tissue from field-caught specimens indicates that vitellogenesis and spermiation commence only after this somatic size threshold is crossed. The age at which this fork length is achieved varies geographically, with individuals in warmer, more productive waters reaching the 80 cm mark several years earlier than those from marginal habitats.

The gonadosomatic index (GSI) of female Cubera snapper reached a mean value of 5.8% [GSI = 5.8%] during the peak spawning period at a water temperature of 25.5 °C [T = 25.5 °C]. This index, representing the proportion of body mass allocated to ovarian tissue, is indicative of a batch-spawning strategy in which multiple clutches are produced over an extended reproductive season. Spawning aggregations are known to form near offshore shelf-edge reefs during the summer months, with gravid females releasing buoyant, fertilised ova into the water column. Fecundity estimates from hydrated oocyte counts range from several hundred thousand to over two million eggs per female per season, depending on body size and condition.

Development begins with the fertilisation of pelagic eggs. At the laboratory incubation temperature of 25.5 °C [T = 25.5 °C], the yolk-sac larva emerges from the chorion after approximately 7.5 days [ab = approximately 7.5 days], a duration typical for tropical lutjanids. The newly hatched prolarva has a wet weight of only 0.00025 grams [Wwb = 0.00025 grams], reflecting the limited endogenous yolk reserves available to support the endotrophic phase. This minuscule birth mass necessitates a rapid transition to exogenous feeding; the first prey capture typically occurs within 48 hours of hatching, coinciding with the functional development of the mouth gape and visual acuity. Larval survival during this critical period is highly dependent upon the availability of suitable zooplanktonic prey, and mortality rates are correspondingly elevated. Field collections of ichthyoplankton suggest that the pelagic larval duration lasts approximately 25 to 30 days before settlement into shallow estuarine nursery habitats.

Maximum longevity in Lutjanus cyanopterus has been estimated from otolith increment analysis, with the oldest individuals reaching an age of 55 years [am = 55 years] in waters maintained at a mean annual temperature of 25.5 °C [T = 25.5 °C]. This extended lifespan, exceeding that of most other Caribbean lutjanids, is a hallmark of a slow-paced life history characterised by late maturity, large adult body size, and iteroparous reproduction. The combination of a 55-year lifespan and a 7.5-day embryonic period illustrates the extraordinary range of temporal scales compressed into the species' life cycle. Senescence in older individuals is marked by reduced somatic condition and declining reproductive output, though the largest females continue to contribute disproportionately to the larval pool through elevated fecundity. These demographic parameters underscore the vulnerability of the species to overfishing, as the removal of large, old individuals can rapidly erode the reproductive potential of the population.
